newsitem.title: INDIA: India may remove import ban on zinc ash - trade.
newsitem.headline: India may remove import ban on zinc ash - trade.

text.p: A year-old ban on imports of zinc ash and waste, which nearly put many small zinc ingot producers out of business, is likely to be ended next week, traders said on Wednesday.
Traders said they expected next Tuesday's announcement of 1997/98 (April/March) export-import policy to remove the ban.
"This move will improve zinc ingot production and help arrest the rise in prices," said Sharad Parikh, president of the Bombay Metals Exchange.
The ban on imports of zinc ash and waste was imposed following charges that small-scale zinc units using these raw materials were violating anti-pollution laws. Producers deny this.
Parikh said the new policy could be in line with the 1997/98 federal budget, which further reduced import tariffs on most items, including non-ferrous metals.
The budget halved import duty on nickel to 10 percent to help the domestic steel industry. It also reduced duty on tin to 20 percent from 30 percent to help the domestic alloy industry.
The budget reduced import duty on concentrates of copper and zinc to five percent from 10 percent to help domestic producers importing raw materials.
Parikh said he would expect Indian non-ferrous metals to remain steady in line with a firm trend on the London Metals Exchange (LME).
Traders expect business volumes to be low in the current week as fiscal 1996/97 draws to a close by end-March.
"The end of the financial year is round the corner and major players are keeping to the sidelines as they are busy with their books of account," Parikh said.
"LME prices are steady. They will not go down," he said. "Indian prices will be firm because of limited imports."
In the week to Wednesday, copper gained 50 rupees to 13,500 rupees per quintal (100 kg). Zinc gained 50 rupees to 7,750.
Tin was up 100 at 31,600.
Nickel lost 200 to 37,100, while aluminium was 75 lower at 7,425.
